content: Vaccinia virus (VACV or VV) is a large, complex, and enveloped virus that belongs to the poxvirus family. It has a linear, double-stranded DNA genome approximately 190 kilobase pairs in length, encoding around 250 genes. This virus is historically significant as it served as the vaccine that eradicated smallpox, marking the first successful eradication of a human disease. This monumental achievement was led by the World Health Organization under the Smallpox Eradication Program. Following the eradication of smallpox, Vaccinia virus has been studied extensively for its potential use in gene therapy and genetic engineering, as it can deliver genes into biological tissues. Additionally, concerns about smallpox being used as a bioterrorism agent have renewed scientific interest in studying this virus. Vaccinia virus is closely related to the cowpox virus, and historically, the two were often considered the same. However, the exact origin of Vaccinia virus remains unclear due to the lack of detailed records during its repeated cultivation and passage in research laboratories over decades. It is widely believed that Vaccinia virus, cowpox virus, and Variola virus (the causative agent of smallpox) share a common ancestral virus. There is also speculation that Vaccinia virus may have originally been isolated from horses. Unlike most DNA viruses, Vaccinia virus replicates exclusively in the cytoplasm of the host cell, rather than in the nucleus. This unique replication strategy necessitates a large genome to encode the enzymes and proteins required for viral DNA replication and gene transcription. During its replication cycle, Vaccinia virus produces four infectious forms, each differing in their outer membranes: intracellular mature virion (IMV), intracellular enveloped virion (IEV), cell-associated enveloped virion (CEV), and extracellular enveloped virion (EEV). The IMV, which has a single lipoprotein membrane, is the most abundant form and is thought to facilitate host-to-host transmission. The CEV, surrounded by two membrane layers, is believed to mediate cell-to-cell spread, while the EEV, also with two membranes, is important for long-range dissemination within the host. The IEV, with three envelopes, plays a role in intracellular transport. These distinctions remain a topic of ongoing research and debate. Vaccinia virus encodes several proteins that confer resistance to interferons, which are critical components of the host immune response. The K3L protein mimics the eukaryotic initiation factor 2-alpha (eIF-2α) and inhibits the action of PKR, a key activator of interferons. Another protein, E3L, also inhibits PKR activation and has the additional ability to bind double-stranded RNA, further suppressing the host's antiviral response. Vaccinia virus infection in humans is generally mild and often asymptomatic in healthy individuals, though it may occasionally cause a mild rash and fever. Importantly, the immune response generated by Vaccinia virus infection provides protection against lethal smallpox infection. For this reason, Vaccinia virus was used as a live-virus vaccine against smallpox. Unlike vaccines that use attenuated forms of the target virus, the Vaccinia vaccine does not contain the smallpox virus itself. However, adverse effects can occur, particularly in immunocompromised individuals, where the risk of severe complications is significantly higher. Fatal responses to the vaccine are rare, occurring in approximately one in one million cases.S. military personnel. Due to the potential threat of smallpox-related bioterrorism, there is a possibility that widespread vaccination may be required again in the future. To address this, scientists are developing safer and more rapidly deployable vaccine strategies. On September 1, 2007, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved a new smallpox vaccine, ACAM2000, which can be produced quickly in response to demand. This vaccine, manufactured by Acambis Inc., is derived from the older Dryvax vaccine and uses Vaccinia virus. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has stockpiled 192.5 million doses of ACAM2000. The concept of vaccination originated with Edward Jenner's work in 1796, when he used cowpox (variolae vaccinae) to protect against smallpox. The term vaccination is derived from the Latin word for cowpox. Over time, it became clear that the virus used in smallpox vaccination was not identical to cowpox, but the name Vaccinia remained associated with the vaccine-related virus. In March 2007, a two-year-old boy in Indiana and his mother contracted a life-threatening Vaccinia infection from the boy's father, who had been vaccinated for smallpox prior to his deployment with the U.S. Army. The child developed a severe rash covering 80% of his body after close contact with his father. The boy's eczema, a known risk factor for Vaccinia infection, likely facilitated the transmission. He was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin, cidofovir, and an experimental drug developed by SIGA Technologies. By April 19, 2007, the child had recovered and was discharged, with the only lasting effect being potential scarring of the skin.
